transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-08-16
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Luca Moretti (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (KelpNet CTO), Priya Iyer (KelpNet ML Eng), Marco Chen (KelpNet SRE)

Auto Summary (auto-generated):
KelpNet is evaluating Redwood for a customer-facing streaming assistant and internal summarization pipelines. Primary concerns: p95 latency targets for streaming responses, burst tolerance at release, and whether Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private makes sense given data residency and KMS requirements. They asked for benchmarks, pricing for reserved burst capacity, and a short runway to run tests.

Topics Covered:
- p95 latency targets and real-world expectations
- concurrency and burst scenarios (simultaneous streaming sessions)
- token/sec and end-to-end throughput benchmarking approach
- hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs (security, KMS, network egress)
- fallback strategies and quantized model variants
- next steps and benchmark scheduling

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Diego, Priya, Marco, um I'm Samira from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Luca, would you like to intro quickly?
[00:08] Luca: Hey all, Luca, Solutions Eng. We'll mostly talk perf, capacity, and the benchmark plan—try not to get too deep into the weeds but we can.
[00:14] Diego: Thanks, Samira. We're trying to understand how Redwood would handle our product launch in Q4, mainly burst-y streaming usage, like 10s to 100s of simultaneous chats that keep streaming tokens back and forth.
[00:26] Priya: Yeah and also internal summarization jobs that are batch-y but high token/sec.
[00:31] Marco: From SRE side, we care about p95 tail and how you handle sudden surges—do you throttle, queue, or spin up capacity?

[00:40] Luca: Good questions. Can you give us target numbers? What's an acceptable p95 for your user flows?
[00:46] Diego: For interactive chat we want p95 under 300ms for small responses (<64 tokens) and under 800ms p95 for 512-token responses when streaming—those are aspirational.
[00:58] Priya: For the summarization batch jobs, maybe throughput of 50k tokens/sec across the fleet during nightly windows.
[01:07] Marco: Peak concurrency: nominally 150 concurrent streams, but during promos we could hit 600 concurrent streams for a few minutes.

[01:18] Samira: Ok that's super helpful. Quick framing: Hosted can hit low latency but is multi-tenant; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput, and Private gives you VPC/on-prem for strict data controls. For burst tolerance we offer burst capacity on Dedicated—it's a paid buffer tied to a burst policy.
[01:38] Diego: Is burst capacity instant? We can't wait 30 seconds for scale-up in the middle of a user session.

[01:44] Luca: Right, we use fast pre-warmed standby and grace queues. For streaming, we recommend a two-tier approach: keep a small dedicated steady pool sized for expected concurrent prefixes, and then configure burst capacity to absorb short spikes. The transition is near-instant—streams are routed to warm workers where possible. Worst case short warm-up adds 50–200ms on a cold path.

[02:06] Marco: That 50–200ms is okay, but if the p95 jumps from 300ms to 800ms for 30s during promos that might be unacceptable. How do we guarantee fallbacks?

[02:15] Luca: We suggest a fallback policy: route to a quantized variant of the same model (4-bit/Q4) or to a smaller distilled model when latency climbs. That typically keeps p95 in the 350–500ms range while saving tokens/cost.

[02:30] Priya: Are quantized model outputs identical? We need quality to not regress too much for user-facing chat.

[02:35] Luca: You will see small differences; we show delta metrics in our Optimize toolkit. We can run A/B evals on your prompt set. In practice for many chat flows the quality delta is negligible.

[02:45] Diego: What about token/sec numbers—can you give examples of observed throughput on your Dedicated pools?

[02:51] Samira: Sure—on a single A100-equivalent worker we often see on the order of 400–800 tokens/sec for decoding workloads depending on sequence length and model. For 8-bit/quantized we can push higher. But you should think in cluster terms: 50k tokens/sec is doable with a small fleet of Dedicated workers and batching/caching.

[03:10] Marco: Ok so if we need 50k tokens/sec during a nightly window, what does that map to in nodes?

[03:14] Luca: Rough rule: assume 500 tokens/sec per GPU for mixed sequences. So 50k tokens/sec ≈ 100 GPUs if you rely on per-request decoding without heavy batching. But with efficient batching and prefix KV cache you can reduce that by 2–4x. So it's workload-dependent—send us traces and we'll run the calc.

[03:35] Priya: We'll share traces. Also question on streaming—how do you measure p95 for streaming responses? Is it first-byte latency or end-to-end?

[03:43] Luca: Good callout. We measure both. For streaming UX people care about first-token latency (TTFB) and the per-chunk inter-arrival. We report p95 first-byte latency and p95 per-chunk latency in the Console. For your targets you probably want p95 first-byte <= 300ms.

[03:58] Diego: And concurrency? How do you recommend sizing the steady-state pool for 150 concurrent streams?

[04:05] Luca: Depends on average tokens/sec per session. If sessions stream at ~5 tokens/sec on average, 150 streams are ~750 tokens/sec. That's under one GPU theoretically, but streaming has per-connection overhead so we usually allocate with concurrency headroom—maybe 2–4 GPUs as steady pool, plus burst.

[04:20] Marco: We also have SSO and KMS constraints: all request logs must be in our VPC and keys in our HSM. That pushes us toward Private. Can Redwood Private integrate with on-prem HSM?

[04:31] Samira: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and can run in your VPC or on-prem package. There's a separate deployment and licensing model—we'll include that in the docs.

[04:39] Priya: If we go Private, do we lose access to Redwood's Console metrics or are those proxied?

[04:45] Luca: The Private control plane can forward metrics into your telemetry stack and we provide a UI endpoint you can host. There are options for metrics retention and trace ingestion.

[04:54] Diego: What about cold-start token cache behavior? We use long dialogs with big KV caches; how are those managed across replicas?

[05:02] Luca: Our runtime manages KV cache per-session on the worker. For streaming with long dialog, you ideally keep a session pinned to a worker or use sticky routing; we support sticky sessions to avoid reloading full KV caches. We also support prefix caching for common contexts. Transcription engine sometimes writes it as K-V cash which is odd, sorry.

[05:20] Priya: (laughs) I've seen the K-V cash typo already.

[05:24] Samira: On the benchmarking side, Luca, what's our plan we recommended?

[05:28] Luca: We'll run three tests: steady-state streaming at target concurrency, synthetic promos (short 5–15 minute spikes to 4x concurrency), and batch token-throughput for summarization. We'll use your prompt set and traffic CSV. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 for first-byte and per-chunk latencies, token/sec, and GPU utilization.

[05:46] Diego: How much time does the engineering bench need?

[05:49] Luca: Two hours to run the harness for the initial pass, then we'll analyze for a day. If you need longer stress tests we'll iterate.

[05:55] Marco: For promos we need deterministic fallbacks: if latency breaches threshold we want to switch to distilled model automatically. Is that supported?

[06:03] Luca: Yes, rollout policies can be configured as automatic fallback rules: threshold on p95 or error-rate triggers fallback to a pinned variant. You can set cooldowns and canary windows.

[06:12] Priya: Do you have telemetry hooks for our APM? We use Datadog and want token-level tracing stitched to traces.

[06:18] Samira: Absolutely, we have tracing hooks and can forward spans to Datadog; we'll include example instrumentation.

[06:24] Diego: Costs—how does Dedicated pricing for steady + burst compare to Hosted? Need unit economics to present to CFO.

[06:30] Samira: Hosted is usage-based and simple; Dedicated is monthly commit for capacity plus burst buffer costs—usually cheaper per token at scale but with some fixed cost. We'll send an example pricing model with cost per steady GPU, per-burst minute, and example amortization for your projected 3-months usage.

[06:46] Marco: Do you bill burst as per-minute or token units?

[06:49] Samira: Typically per-minute for reserved burst capacity plus token usage; again we'll show the calculator that maps to your traffic.

[06:56] Diego: One more item on security—audit logs must be tamper-evident and kept for 1 year. Is that available on Dedicated/Private?

[07:03] Luca: Yes, audit logging is available on Dedicated and Private. Private gives you the easiest path to keep logs entirely inside your environment; Dedicated can forward logs to your storage with encryption in transit.

[07:12] Priya: Any caveats for multi-region? We'll have users in EU and NA.

[07:17] Luca: We recommend region-aware routing with a primary region per user for latency, plus DR region for failover. For strict residency you can use Private in EU.

[07:26] Diego: Okay, can we talk specifics: we have a sample peak day where we saw 480 concurrent streams with avg token rate 4 tps, and bursts to 1.8k streams for 3 minutes during our campaign.

[07:38] Luca: That's useful. If average rate is 4 tokens/sec per stream, 480 streams ~= 1920 tokens/sec steady, bursts to 1800 streams ~= 7200 tokens/sec. That is small relative to 50k tokens/sec but concurrency overhead is the challenge. For streaming, plan steady reserve to cover 600–800 streams and burst buffer for the promo moments.

[07:59] Marco: For the promo bursts we want 99% requests to succeed without fallback. Is that feasible?

[08:05] Luca: We can get close with large burst buffers but 99% without any fallback requires significant overprovisioning. We typically combine a large burst buffer for short windows with automatic fallback to keep user experience stable.

[08:18] Samira: We'll provide a sizing note showing three options: conservative (no fallbacks, more reserved capacity), balanced (moderate reserve + fallback), and cost-optimized (smaller reserve + fallback + quantized variants).

[08:29] Priya: Great. Also we're interested in the exact metrics you'll provide post-bench.

[08:33] Luca: We'll provide per-endpoint CSVs: timestamps, request id, first_byte_ms, last_byte_ms, token_count, gpu_id, worker_id, model_variant. We'll also give aggregated p50/p95/p99 and histograms.

[08:46] Diego: Cool, can you also include a sample of the routing policy ASM? I recall a yaml example in your docs but couldn't find it.

[08:54] Samira: I'll attach the routing example in the follow-up email—it's a short YAML snippet for fallback thresholds and region routing.

[09:00] Marco: One more about cold cache—if a session is rebalanced to a different worker during a long dialog, how long to reload the KV?

[09:07] Luca: Depends on history size, but restoring a 2–4K token KV cache can take a few hundred ms to a second. Sticky routing avoids that. For super long dialogues we recommend session affinity.

[09:18] Priya: (overlap) Are there limits on simultaneous streaming chunk sizes? We stream 32-token chunks every ~200ms.

[09:24] Luca: That's fine; the runtime is optimized for small chunks. We surface per-chunk latency in the Console so you can tune chunk size.

[09:31] Diego: Ok, I'm trying to think of blockers—data residency points to Private, cost points to Dedicated. We probably want a pilot on Dedicated with a Private evaluation for later.

[09:41] Samira: That's a common path—pilot Dedicated, then if regs require, move to Private. We can structure a short Dedicated pilot with a path to Private.

[09:49] Diego: Timelines—if we start a pilot the week of Aug 24, can you run bench and give sizing by Aug 28?

[09:56] Luca: Yes, if you provide prompt sets and traces by Aug 20 I can run the harness and get results by Aug 28.

[10:02] Priya: We'll aim to upload the artifacts by Friday.

[10:05] Samira: Great. Any other technical Qs?

[10:07] Marco: One operational: do you charge for testbed GPUs during benchmark runs?

[10:11] Samira: For pilot runs we include a small amount of test time in the pilot; large scale load tests beyond the pilot window may be billed—I'll note details in the pricing doc.

[10:20] Diego: And finally, do you have examples of customers with similar burst patterns?

[10:24] Samira: We do—I'll include anonymized case studies. One had similar promos and used balanced reserve+fallback to keep p95 stable while reducing cost 35% vs naive overprovision.

[10:33] Diego: perfect.

[10:35] (brief cross-talk, small audio glitch)

[10:40] Samira: OK quick recap: Samira sends Dedicated pricing + routing YAML + case studies by Aug 18; Luca runs benchmark harness after KelpNet uploads traces and sample prompts; Diego/Team to upload by Aug 20; follow-up bench results by Aug 28. Any changes?

[10:58] Priya: Sounds right. Also can Luca include a recommended fallback threshold example?

[11:02] Luca: Yep, I'll include example thresholds (p95 first-byte > 350ms for 30s -> fallback to quantized).

[11:09] Diego: Thanks everyone. We'll sync after the bench.

[11:14] Samira: Thanks, everyone. We'll follow up in email with links: pricing sheet (link), benchmark harness repo (link), shared drive for artifacts (link).

[11:23] End of meeting.
